note: For each domain: the eight steps of the workflow and the performing and ownership conditions for the eight judgment axes. Items, the results report and experience input all read this one file. `verify_targets` and `artifacts` are what the results report's action steps draw on, so they must be concrete here to avoid vague wording

workflow.name: How the problem arrives
workflow.detail: What people want arrives as a verbal description or a screen sketch

workflow.name: Inputs received
workflow.detail: Stakeholder requirements, constraints of existing systems, deadline and team size

workflow.name: What gets decided first
workflow.detail: What is out of scope this time, and the lines that separate modules

workflow.name: Methods used
workflow.detail: Writing user flows, dividing responsibilities, writing contracts, comparing the cost of change

workflow.name: Tools used
workflow.detail: Diagramming tools, a document repository, a dependency analyzer, meeting notes

workflow.name: Deliverables produced
workflow.detail: Requirements list, module diagram, interface contracts, decision records

workflow.name: What it is compared against
workflow.detail: Requirements list, existing system architecture, similar cases, number of changes after implementation

workflow.name: When it goes wrong
workflow.detail: If fixing one place forces changes in several modules, redraw the boundaries

J1.l2: I wrote down what this system would cover within the given topic
J1.l3: The scope I drew became the development scope as is

J2.l2: I turned requirements into conditions to meet and metrics
J2.l3: The conditions I set were used as acceptance criteria

J3.l2: I set the lines between modules and the direction of dependencies
J3.l3: The code was split along the boundaries I set, and they held

J4.l2: I chose and used a method and tool for describing the structure
J4.l3: The way I chose to describe the structure became the team default

J5.l2: I documented the module diagram and interface contracts
J5.l3: Someone else implemented from the contracts I left

J6.l2: I compared two designs by the cost of change
J6.l3: I changed the design based on the comparison

J7.l2: When fixing one place, I found and narrowed down the modules that changed with it
J7.l3: After redrawing the boundaries, I confirmed that the scope of changes shrank

J8.l2: I presented a design in a review meeting and explained it
J8.l3: My design decisions were used for the development schedule and staffing

org_outcomes.OC1: A structure that can be maintained for years, and its operating cost
org_outcomes.OC2: Contracts that customers can adopt and use
org_outcomes.OC3: Design deliverables that meet the acceptance criteria
org_outcomes.OC4: Architecture design as a project deliverable
org_outcomes.OC5: A design written so the method can be reproduced
org_outcomes.OC6: Design reasoning that can show compliance with standards
org_outcomes.OC7: A structure that can be changed quickly and thrown away

domains.name: Data Structures and Algorithms

workflow.name: How the problem arrives
workflow.detail: The size of the data to process and the time it must take arrive as constraints

workflow.name: Inputs received
workflow.detail: Input size and distribution, memory limits, acceptable response time

workflow.name: What gets decided first
workflow.detail: How to represent the data, and which operations to make fast

workflow.name: Methods used
workflow.detail: Calculating complexity, comparing data representations, testing edge-case inputs, comparing measured results

workflow.name: Tools used
workflow.detail: Complexity analysis notes, performance measurement tools, test input generators, memory profilers

workflow.name: Deliverables produced
workflow.detail: Implementation code, complexity reasoning notes, performance measurement records, edge-case input tests

workflow.name: What it is compared against
workflow.detail: Theoretical complexity, measured time, results from other representations, existing implementations

workflow.name: When it goes wrong
workflow.detail: If it's slow, narrow the cause down to data representation, iteration count or memory access

verify_targets: Results with a different data structure

J1.l2: I wrote the computational problem to solve in terms of inputs and outputs
J1.l3: The problem definition I set determined the implementation scope

J2.l2: I wrote the allowed time and memory limits as numbers
J2.l3: The limits I set were used as design criteria

J3.l2: I decided how to represent the data and which operations to make fast
J3.l3: The implementation settled on the representation I chose

J4.l2: I calculated the complexity and chose a measurement method
J4.l3: The measurement method I set became the team standard

J5.l2: I left the implementation code together with the complexity reasoning
J5.l3: Someone else took and used the implementation I left

J6.l2: I compared theoretical complexity with measured time on the same input
J6.l3: I changed the data representation based on the comparison

J7.l2: I narrowed down the cause of a slow section to iteration count and memory access
J7.l3: I fixed the cause I found and confirmed the time went down

J8.l2: I explained performance comparison results to the team
J8.l3: My performance reasoning was used to decide which features to add or drop

org_outcomes.OC1: Response time users feel, and server cost
org_outcomes.OC2: Processing limits that hold in customer environments too
org_outcomes.OC3: An implementation that met the required performance within the deadline
org_outcomes.OC4: Project performance targets and the reasoning behind them
org_outcomes.OC5: Complexity proofs and experiments for a new method
org_outcomes.OC6: Evidence for judging compliance with performance standards
org_outcomes.OC7: The simplest implementation that holds up at the current data volume

review_note: Computer science and software covers work inside a single machine, work between machines, and screens that people look at, all in one file. What keeps them apart is `required_axes`: design work depends on requirements interpretation, distributed and systems work on failure and correction, and algorithm and learning work on comparison and verification
